title: Spray blocking
subtitle: Dampening and pinning without full immersion — the quick method for many fibre types
excerpt: Spray blocking uses a water mist to relax the fibres just enough to pin the piece to measurements. Faster than wet blocking and gentler than steam. The right method for wool, plant fibres, and many blends when the piece doesn't need aggressive opening.
sourceNotes: Pauline Turner, How to Crochet — finishing and blocking. Standard British crochet finishing techniques.

glossaryTerms.definition: A small hand-pump spray bottle filled with clean cold water, used to mist a crochet piece evenly for spray blocking.
Placing blocking pins at key points (corners, edges, curve peaks) to hold the piece at the specified finished dimensions while it dries.

heroPrompt: A crochet square pinned to a grey foam blocking mat at its four corners, with a small spray bottle visible beside it. The piece is slightly damp, with pins at even intervals along the edges.

content.text: Spray blocking is the simplest blocking method: lay the piece on a mat, mist it lightly with water from a
, and pin it to the correct finished measurements. The water relaxes the fibres without fully saturating them, which is gentler on the twist of the yarn and means a shorter drying time.
Lay the piece face-up on a foam blocking mat. Do not stretch it yet.
Mist the piece evenly with clean cold water. The yarn should be visibly damp but not saturated — you should not be able to squeeze water out of it.
Gently smooth the piece to roughly the finished dimensions using your hands.
at the corners and midpoints of each edge. Use a tape measure and the schematic measurements as the guide, not how the piece looks by eye.
Fill in additional pins along the edges, spaced about 3-4 cm apart, keeping the edge straight.
Leave to dry completely — at least 4 hours at room temperature, longer in a cool or humid room. Remove pins only when fully dry.
Wool and wool blends that aren't superwash: the natural fibre responds quickly to even light moisture.
Plant fibres (cotton, linen, bamboo) for pieces that need straightening but not aggressive opening of lace.
Granny squares and motifs that need to be flattened and squared before joining.
When to use wet blocking or steam instead

Lace that needs the pattern opened fully: wet blocking provides more relaxation than spray. Tightly-worked natural fibre pieces that have strong memory: wet blocking gives deeper penetration. Pieces that need heat to set: steam blocking. Acrylic and synthetic blends: these need specific handling — see the guide on blocking synthetic fibres.
